headline: UAE-Saudi cooperation pact to re-enter conflict
dek: UAE agreed a cooperation pact with Saudi Arabia to re-enter the Yemen conflict amid Ansar Allah advances; STC leader Zubaidi fled to Abu Dhabi after the Aden incident and the Saudi-backed government threatened to try him for treason; STC called for a referendum to restore 1967–1990 South Yemen borders;…
fault_line: Should South Yemen secede again — or is the coalition fracturing exactly when it needs unity?

sections.what_happened: The United Arab Emirates has agreed a cooperation pact with Saudi Arabia to re-enter the Yemen conflict, as Ansar Allah's advances reshape the battlefield. The Southern Transitional Council's leader, Aidarus al-Zubaidi, has fled to Abu Dhabi after the Aden incident, with the Saudi-backed government threatening to try him for treason. The STC has called for a referendum to restore the nineteen sixty-seven to nineteen ninety borders of South Yemen. The Emirates has resumed support for the Giant Brigades, the southern forces. Aden airport was hit on Friday by two Ansar Allah missiles, according to Yemeni government statements.
sections.what_verified: Two outlets carry the pact, the Zubaidi flight, the treason threat and the Giant Brigades thread. The Friday missile strikes on Aden airport are corroborated by Yemeni government statements and earlier coverage. What is not confirmed: neither Riyadh nor Abu Dhabi has officially responded to the STC's referendum demand, and the details of the Aden incident itself come from the government side only. The cooperation pact is reported by two outlets — solid, but not yet an official announcement from either capital.
sections.what_disputed: The STC's secession referendum demand is a political claim, not an agreed process — no capital has endorsed it, and the Saudi-backed government's treason threat against Zubaidi shows how explosive it is. The exact circumstances of Zubaidi's flight to Abu Dhabi, and what the 'cooperation pact' commits the Emirates to in practice, are not yet public. The Aden airport strikes are attributed to Ansar Allah by the Yemeni government; Ansar Allah has not been quoted confirming them in the material reviewed.
sections.why_matters: The anti-Ansar Allah coalition is doing two opposite things at once: expanding and fracturing. The Emirates is back in, Egypt is reportedly weighing entry — the war is widening. But the STC's secession push threatens to split the 'united' front the moment it widens. A coalition that cannot agree on whether South Yemen should exist as a separate state is a coalition that can barely agree on a war plan. Zubaidi fleeing to Abu Dhabi while facing treason charges from the government Abu Dhabi is now pact-bound to support is the contradiction, made flesh.
sections.context: South Yemen was an independent state from nineteen sixty-seven to nineteen ninety, and the secessionist current never died — the STC has governed the separatist cause in Aden for years. The Emirates previously backed southern forces including the Giant Brigades before drawing down. Ansar Allah's advances have now pulled Abu Dhabi back toward the fight, but on terms that empower the very southern separatists the Saudi-backed government in Aden considers traitors. Every previous round of this war has shown the same pattern: the anti-Ansar Allah camp's internal fractures do as much damage as Ansar Allah's missiles.

totw_analysis: Watch the shape of this, not just the headlines. The coalition against Ansar Allah is getting bigger — the Emirates re-entering, Egypt circling — and simultaneously less coherent. That is not a paradox; it is the story. Zubaidi runs to Abu Dhabi for safety while the government Abu Dhabi just signed a pact with calls him a traitor. The STC demands a referendum on restoring South Yemen while the coalition it belongs to insists Yemen must stay whole. These are not teething problems. They are the structural cracks that Ansar Allah has exploited for a decade: every time the coalition masses against the north, the south reminds everyone it never signed up for a united Yemen in the first place. The Western coverage will frame this as the coalition regrouping — note the framing, and note what it hides. A regrouping that includes a secession referendum and a treason trial is not a regrouping. It is a holding action while the partners negotiate what they are even fighting for. The honest question, and the one our audience is already arguing: if South Yemen secedes, does the war against Ansar Allah get simpler — or does the coalition just lose the south while still losing the north? There are two defensible answers, which is exactly why this story will run.
